prime.problem: Saying ‘this query is slow’ from one run on one database can't tell you how it will grow. You need to know which input is growing (the data or the query) and how cost scales with it.
prime.fits: Fourth card of the batch and queries part. It builds on cs-1's big-O and on the previous card's multi-hop queries, and it sets up the next card: recursive (fixpoint) queries are PTIME-complete.
expect: data vs expression vs combined complexity
prime.goal: Place a query language in a complexity class under data complexity, compute how a query's work grows as n or k grows, and explain why data complexity is the usual lens.

attend: For a query with k variables over n values, why is the work n<sup>k</sup> but the memory only k·⌈log₂ n⌉ bits?
Why does doubling n multiply the triangle query's work by 8, while adding one variable multiplies it by n?
Why must a completeness reduction be weaker than the class itself?
How does each quantifier of a relational-calculus query turn into one gate, and why does that put CALC in AC⁰?
When is data complexity the wrong lens, even for a database?

must: Evaluate a k-variable query with one pointer per variable → k nested loops over n values → n<sup>k</sup> assignments tried but only k·⌈log₂ n⌉ bits of state → CALC is in LOGSPACE
Hold the query fixed and grow the data → k is a constant → the work is a polynomial of degree k (×2³ = 8 per doubling for k = 3) → data complexity is polynomial or better for fixed joins
Hold the data fixed and grow the query → the work multiplies by n per extra variable → expression complexity is exponential in the query (CALC PSPACE-complete, conjunctive queries NP-complete)
Databases dwarf queries → data complexity is the usual lens → it separates CALC (AC⁰) from fixpoint queries (PTIME-complete) from while (PSPACE-complete)
elevated: Each quantifier becomes one unbounded fan-in gate (∃ = OR, ∀ = AND) → circuit depth depends on the query, not the data → constant depth, so CALC ⊆ AC⁰, and parity (not in AC⁰) is beyond it
reference: Savitch's theorem and the space hierarchy

compress.prompt: Close the card and draw the nested classes with one example query in each. Next to it, write the two growth rules (per doubling of n, per extra variable) with the triangle numbers, and one sentence on why data complexity is the default.
checklist: AC⁰ inside LOGSPACE inside PTIME inside NP inside PSPACE
fixed query: ×2<sup>k</sup> per doubling of n (×8 for triangles)
fixed data: ×n per extra variable (×10 at n = 10)
queries are small, data is large, so fix the query

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between data complexity and expression complexity using the triangle query on the ring database.
answer: data: fix k = 3, grow n; work n³ grows ×8 per doubling
expression: fix n = 10, grow k; work 10<sup>k</sup> grows ×10 per variable
same evaluator, different input held fixed

retrieve.q: Walk through why the triangle query finds 60 answers at n = 10 on the ring, and why k = 4 finds none but still tries 10,000 assignments.
answer: each consecutive triple {i, i+1, i+2} is a triangle: n = 10 of them
the ring has no 4 mutual friends, but nested loops try every assignment regardless: 10⁴

retrieve.q: An ORM generates 100-way joins. Argue why the ‘fixed query’ assumption fails and what theory or engine techniques apply instead.
answer: k is large, so n<sup>k</sup> matters and data complexity misleads
combined complexity and query width: acyclic or bounded-treewidth queries stay polynomial in k
worst-case-optimal joins and good join ordering

compare.q: This card places fixpoint queries in PTIME; the next shows how engines evaluate them. What guarantees the fixpoint arrives in polynomially many rounds, and what does semi-naïve change about the work per round, not the class?
answer: facts are never removed and at most n<sup>k</sup> exist for an arity-k predicate, so the loop stops within polynomially many rounds
semi-naïve joins only last round's new facts
same class (PTIME), far less work: 70 → 15 derivations on the 6-node chain

compare.q: Big-O measures one algorithm; a complexity class measures a whole query language. What does each let you conclude, and what does each hide?
answer: big-O: the growth of a specific algorithm's cost
class: the best any algorithm can do for the hardest query in a language, in the worst case
big-O hides constants; a class also hides that ‘in PTIME’ allows n³, which at 10⁷ rows is 10²¹ steps

predict.q: Evaluate the same triangle query on the ring with an index: for each ordered edge (x, y), look only at y's neighbours z and check (x, z). Commit first: does the query's complexity class change, and roughly how many checks does it do at n = 80?
predict.answer: The class doesn't change: it's a property of the language's hardest queries, not of one evaluator. The work does: the ring has 4 neighbours per person, so 4n ordered edges × 4 neighbours = 16n checks, 1,280 at n = 80 against the nested loops' 512,000 tries. That's the gap between the textbook evaluator and what indexes and hash joins buy.

apply.task: Extend both growth tables by hand one more row. Data complexity: the triangle query (k = 3) at n = 160, giving tries, answers and pointer bits. Expression complexity: k = 7 at n = 10, giving tries and pointer bits. Then check with clique_query and pointer_bits in code/query-complexity-classes.py (skip running k = 7: 10⁷ tries takes a while).
apply.done: n = 160: 160³ = 4,096,000 tries (×8 again), 6 × 160 = 960 answers, 3 × ⌈log₂ 160⌉ = 3 × 8 = 24 bits. k = 7 at n = 10: 10⁷ tries (×10), 7 × 4 = 28 bits, and 0 answers because the ring has no 7 mutual friends.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: whether an index changes the class?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why memory stays logarithmic while work is polynomial?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: variables k → exponent, or class → real running time?
Could you name a query your own system runs where k is large enough that expression complexity matters?
What will you look for in the semi-naïve card: how a PTIME fixpoint is computed without redoing work?
